title: Helpful Microbes
summary: How tiny living things called microbes help people digest food, make bread and yogurt, enrich the soil, and fight disease.
poll: Most germs and microbes are bad for people.

versions.title: Tiny Life Helps Us
versions.text:
Some life is too small to see. It is a microbe. You need a tool to see it.

Some microbes can make us sick. But most do no harm. A lot of them help us!

One kind of microbe is bacteria. Lots of bacteria live in your gut. They help break down food. They help keep bad germs out.

Yeast is a microbe, too. It is used to make bread. Yeast makes gas. The gas makes the bread puff up.

Bacteria help make yogurt. They turn milk thick and sour. Laban is made this way, too.

Microbes live in soil. They break down dead leaves. This makes the soil good for plants.

A mold gave us a drug that kills bad germs. It has saved lots of lives.

So wash your hands well. That gets rid of bad germs. But do not fear all microbes. Most are our friends.

Some microbes can make us sick. But most of them do no harm. Many of them help us!

Yeast is a microbe, too. Bakers use yeast to make bread. Yeast gives off gas. The gas makes the dough puff up.

Bacteria help us make yogurt. They turn milk thick and a bit sour. Laban is made in the same way.

Microbes live in soil, too. They break down dead leaves and plants. This makes the soil rich, so new plants can grow.

Long ago, a man found that a mold could kill bad germs. That mold gave us a new drug. It has saved lots of lives.

So wash your hands well. That gets rid of bad germs. But do not fear all microbes. Most of them are our friends.

versions.title: Helpful Microbes
versions.text:
All around you, there are living things too small to see. They are on your skin, in the air, and in the ground. You need a special tool to see them. These tiny living things are called microbes.

Some microbes can make people sick. But most microbes are not harmful at all. In fact, many of them help us every day.

One kind of microbe is called bacteria. Huge numbers of bacteria live in your gut. They help break down the food you eat. They also make some vitamins and help keep bad germs away.

Yeast is another kind of microbe. Bakers mix yeast into bread dough. The yeast gives off tiny bubbles of gas. The bubbles make the dough rise and get soft.

Bacteria help make yogurt, too. They turn milk thick and a little sour. Laban is made in the same way.

Many microbes live in the soil. They break down dead leaves and plants. This puts good things back into the soil, so new plants can grow.

In 1928, a scientist saw that a mold could kill germs. That mold led to a new medicine. It has saved millions of lives.

So keep washing your hands to get rid of bad germs. But remember that most microbes are our friends.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming saw that a mold could kill germs. That mold led to a medicine. It has saved millions of lives.

versions.title: Helpful Microbes
versions.text:
Living things are all around you, even when you cannot see them. They are on your skin, in the air, and deep in the ground. They are so small that you need a microscope to see them. These tiny living things are called microbes. In the 1670s, a Dutch man named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built his own lenses and became one of the first people to see them.

Some microbes can make people sick. But most microbes are harmless, and many of them are so helpful that we could not live well without them.

One kind of microbe is called bacteria. Trillions of bacteria live in your gut. They help you digest parts of food that your body cannot break down alone. They also make some vitamins, such as vitamin K, and they crowd out harmful germs.

Yeast is a tiny fungus. Bakers mix it into bread dough. The yeast feeds on sugar and gives off a gas called carbon dioxide. Bubbles of this gas get trapped in the dough, so the bread rises.

Other bacteria help people make yogurt and cheese. They feed on the sugar in milk and make an acid. The acid turns the milk thick and a little sour. Laban, a popular drink in Saudi Arabia, is made the same way.

In the soil, many microbes are decomposers. They break down dead leaves, plants, and animals. This returns nutrients to the soil, so new plants can grow.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming saw that a mold could kill bacteria. That mold led to penicillin, the first medicine of its kind. It has saved millions of lives.

So keep washing your hands to get rid of harmful germs. But remember that most microbes are our partners, not our enemies.

Living things surround you everywhere, even though you cannot see them. They live on your skin, drift through the air, and fill the ground beneath your feet. Because they are far too small for the human eye, scientists need a microscope to study them. These tiny organisms are called microbes. In the 1670s, a Dutch shopkeeper named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own powerful lenses and became one of the first people to observe them.

Some microbes cause disease. However, most microbes are harmless, and a great many are so helpful that people could not live healthy lives without them.

One important group of microbes is bacteria. Trillions of bacteria live in your gut, where they help you digest fiber and other parts of food that your body cannot break down by itself. They also produce certain vitamins, including vitamin K, and they crowd out harmful germs that might make you sick.

Yeast is a tiny fungus. When bakers mix it into dough, the yeast feeds on sugar and releases a gas called carbon dioxide. Bubbles of this gas become trapped in the stretchy dough, which causes the bread to rise.

Other bacteria help people make yogurt and cheese because they feed on the natural sugar in milk and produce an acid, which thickens the milk and gives it a slightly sour flavor. Laban, a popular drink in Saudi Arabia, is made through a similar process.

In the soil, many microbes act as decomposers. They break down dead leaves, plants, and animals, returning valuable nutrients to the soil so that new plants can grow.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing in his laboratory could kill bacteria. His discovery led to penicillin, the first medicine of its kind, which has since saved millions of lives.

So continue washing your hands to remove harmful germs. But remember that most microbes are our partners, not our enemies.

Some microbes cause disease, which is why many people think of them only as germs. However, most microbes are completely harmless, and a great many are so extremely helpful that human beings could not live healthy lives without them.

They also produce certain vitamins, including vitamin K, and they crowd out harmful germs that might otherwise make you sick.

In the soil, many microbes act as decomposers. They break down dead leaves, plants, and animals, returning valuable nutrients to the soil so that new plants can grow.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing in his laboratory could destroy bacteria. His discovery eventually led to penicillin, the first medicine of its kind, which has since saved millions of lives.

So continue washing your hands carefully to remove dangerous germs. But remember that most microbes are valuable partners, not dangerous enemies.

versions.title: Helpful Microbes: Our Invisible Partners
versions.text:
Living things surround you everywhere, even though you cannot see them. They live on your skin, drift through the air, and fill the soil beneath your feet. Because they are far too small for the human eye to detect, scientists need a microscope to study these tiny organisms, which are called microorganisms, or microbes. In the 1670s, a Dutch shopkeeper named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own powerful lenses and became one of the first people to observe them, describing them as tiny moving "animals."

Although some microbes cause disease, which is why many people think of them only as germs, most microorganisms are harmless, and a great many are so helpful that human beings could not live healthy lives without them.

Trillions of bacteria live in your gut, where they help you digest fiber and other parts of food that your body cannot break down by itself. They also produce certain vitamins, including vitamin K, and they crowd out harmful germs that might otherwise make you sick.

People have also used microbes to make food for thousands of years through a process called fermentation. In bread dough, a microscopic fungus called yeast feeds on sugar and releases carbon dioxide gas, and bubbles of this gas cause the bread to rise. In yogurt and cheese, bacteria consume the natural sugar in milk and produce an acid that thickens the milk and gives it a slightly sour flavor. Laban, a popular drink in Saudi Arabia, is made through a similar process.

In the soil, many microbes act as decomposers, breaking down dead leaves, plants, and animals and returning valuable nutrients to the ground. Certain bacteria live inside small lumps on the roots of beans and peas, where they take nitrogen from the air and change it into a form that plants can use to grow.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing in his laboratory could destroy bacteria. His discovery led to penicillin, the first antibiotic, which has since saved millions of lives. Doctors warn, however, that using antibiotics when they are not needed can help harmful bacteria become resistant to them.

So continue washing your hands carefully to remove dangerous germs. But remember that most microbes are valuable partners, not enemies.

Although some microbes cause disease, which explains why many people consider them only as dangerous germs, the majority of microorganisms are harmless, and a great many are so beneficial that human beings could not maintain healthy lives without them.

Trillions of bacteria inhabit the human digestive system, where they help you digest fiber and other components of food that your body cannot break down independently. versions.title: Helpful Microbes: Our Invisible Partners
versions.text:
Living organisms surround you everywhere, even though you cannot perceive their presence, because they inhabit your skin, drift through the atmosphere, and populate the soil beneath your feet. Since they are far too small for the human eye to detect, scientists require a microscope to study these minute organisms, which are called microorganisms, or microbes. In the 1670s, a Dutch shopkeeper named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own remarkably powerful lenses and became one of the first individuals to observe them, describing them enthusiastically as tiny moving "animals."

Some microbes cause disease, which explains why many people consider them exclusively as dangerous germs. However, the overwhelming majority of microorganisms are harmless, and a great many are so beneficial that human beings could not maintain healthy lives without them.

Trillions of bacteria inhabit the human digestive system, where they help you digest fiber and other components of food that your body cannot break down independently. These bacteria additionally manufacture certain vitamins, including vitamin K, and they crowd out harmful germs that might otherwise cause illness.

Humans have also relied on microbes to prepare food for thousands of years through a process called fermentation. In bread dough, a microscopic fungus called yeast consumes sugar and releases carbon dioxide gas, and the bubbles of this gas become trapped in the elastic dough, causing the bread to rise, while in yogurt and cheese, bacteria consume the natural sugar in milk and generate an acid that thickens the milk and gives it a slightly sour flavor. Laban, a popular traditional beverage in Saudi Arabia, is created through a comparable process.

In the soil, numerous microbes function as decomposers, breaking down dead leaves, plants, and animals and returning valuable nutrients to the ground for future generations of plants, and certain bacteria live inside small swellings on the roots of beans and peas, where they capture nitrogen from the atmosphere and convert it into a form that plants can absorb and use for growth.

In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing accidentally in his laboratory could destroy bacteria. His observation eventually led to the development of penicillin, the first antibiotic, which has since saved millions of lives. Doctors caution, however, that using antibiotics unnecessarily can help harmful bacteria become resistant to these essential medicines.

Consequently, you should continue washing your hands thoroughly to eliminate dangerous germs, but remember that most microbes are valuable partners rather than enemies.

keyWords.definition: a living thing that is too small to see with your eyes alone
keyWords.example: The nurse said a microbe on the door handle could spread a cold.

keyWords.definition: very tiny living things made of one cell; some help us and some make us sick
keyWords.example: The scientist looked at the bacteria on a glass slide.

keyWords.definition: a tiny living thing that bakers use to make bread soft and puffy
keyWords.example: My aunt adds yeast and warm water to the flour.

keyWords.definition: a thick, slightly sour food made from milk
keyWords.example: I ate a bowl of yogurt with dates for breakfast.

keyWords.definition: the top layer of the ground where plants grow
keyWords.example: We put the seeds into the wet soil and covered them.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Why people should stay away from all germs
How tiny microbes help people and plants
How to bake bread at home
Why soil is brown
questions.why: The whole article tells the many ways microbes help us: in the gut, in food, in the soil, and in medicine.

wrong.A: The article says most microbes do no harm, so it does not tell us to stay away from all of them.
wrong.C: Bread is only one example of how microbes help.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about the color of soil.

questions.stem: Where do lots of helpful bacteria live in your body?
options: In your hair
In your bones
In your eyes
In your gut
questions.why: The article says lots of bacteria live in your gut and help break down food.

wrong.A: The article does not say bacteria live in your hair.
wrong.B: The article does not mention bones.
wrong.C: The article does not mention eyes.

questions.stem: What makes bread dough puff up?
options: Gas made by yeast
Salt in the flour
Cold water
A mold
questions.why: The article says yeast makes gas, and the gas makes the dough puff up.

wrong.B: The article does not say salt makes bread rise.
wrong.C: The article does not say cold water makes bread rise.
wrong.D: The mold in the article was used to make a medicine, not bread.

questions.stem: What do microbes in the soil do?
options: They eat the seeds
They make the soil dry
They break down dead leaves
They keep rain away
questions.why: The article says microbes in soil break down dead leaves, which makes the soil good for plants.

wrong.A: The article does not say microbes eat seeds.
wrong.B: The article does not say microbes make soil dry.
wrong.D: Microbes have nothing to do with rain in the article.

questions.stem: The article says most microbes are our "friends." What does it mean here?
options: They play games with us
They talk to us
They help us
They look like us
questions.why: The article calls microbes friends because many of them help us, like helping us digest food and make bread and yogurt.

wrong.D: Microbes are far too small to look like people.

questions.stem: Which food would NOT be made the way laban is made?
options: A glass of plain water
Yogurt
Cheese made from milk
Thick, sour milk
questions.why: Laban and yogurt are made when bacteria change milk. Plain water has no milk, so bacteria do not make it.

wrong.B: The article says bacteria help make yogurt the same way as laban.
wrong.C: Cheese is also made from milk with help from bacteria.
wrong.D: Bacteria turn milk thick and sour, which is how laban is made.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about yogurt, bread, and soil?
options: To show that microbes are hard to find
To give examples of how microbes help
To teach a recipe for bread
To warn that food can make you sick
questions.why: Each example shows a different way microbes help people or plants.

wrong.A: The examples are about helping, not about finding microbes.
wrong.C: The article does not give the steps of a recipe.
wrong.D: The examples show good things microbes do, not ways food makes us sick.

questions.stem: Why does the article still tell us to wash our hands?
options: Because all microbes are bad
Because soap feeds good microbes
Because water makes bread rise
Because some microbes can make us sick
questions.why: The article says some microbes can make us sick, so washing hands gets rid of those bad germs.

wrong.A: The article says most microbes are friends, not that all are bad.
wrong.B: The article does not say soap feeds microbes.
wrong.C: Washing hands has nothing to do with bread rising.

LOW.prompt: Pick two ways that microbes help people. Write two or three sentences that tell about each one.
checklist: I named two ways microbes help.
I used facts from the article.
I used the word microbe or bacteria.
LOW.modelAnswer: One way microbes help people is that bacteria living in our gut help us digest our food and make vitamins. Another way is that yeast helps bakers make bread rise, and other bacteria help turn milk into yogurt. Microbes in the soil also break down dead leaves and return nutrients so new plants can grow. These tiny microbes do a lot of helpful work.

keyWords.definition: a tool that makes very small things look much bigger
keyWords.example: Under the microscope, a drop of pond water was full of moving dots.
The little lizard in the garden is harmless.

keyWords.definition: to break down food in the body so it can be used
keyWords.example: It takes a few hours to digest a big lunch.

keyWords.definition: a living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals
keyWords.example: Mushrooms are decomposers that grow on old logs.

keyWords.definition: something in food or soil that living things need to grow and stay healthy
keyWords.example: Spinach has many nutrients that help your body.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Microbes are tiny, but most of them help people and the planet in important ways.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the greatest scientist in history.
Bread is a healthier food than yogurt because bakers use yeast to make it.
All bacteria cause disease, so every one of them must be destroyed quickly.
questions.why: The article explains how microbes help us digest food, make bread and yogurt, return nutrients to soil, and fight disease.

wrong.B: Van Leeuwenhoek is a supporting detail, and the article does not make this claim.
wrong.C: The article does not compare which food is healthier.
wrong.D: The article says most microbes are harmless or helpful.

questions.stem: What gas does yeast give off in bread dough?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Steam
questions.why: The article says yeast feeds on sugar and gives off carbon dioxide, and the bubbles make bread rise.

wrong.A: The article does not say yeast gives off oxygen.
wrong.B: Nitrogen is not mentioned as the gas in bread.
wrong.D: The article names carbon dioxide, not steam.

questions.stem: Besides helping you digest food, what else do gut bacteria do?
options: They help your bones grow longer
They make some vitamins and crowd out harmful germs
They turn sugar into gas inside bread
They let your eyes see clearly when the room is very dark
questions.why: The article says gut bacteria make vitamins such as vitamin K and crowd out harmful germs.

wrong.A: The article does not mention bones.
wrong.C: Yeast, not gut bacteria, makes gas in bread dough.
wrong.D: The article does not mention eyesight.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: "This returns nutrients to the soil, so new plants can grow." What does returns mean here?
options: Takes away
Hides
Measures
Gives back
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead things and give their nutrients back to the soil.

wrong.A: Taking nutrients away would not help new plants grow.
wrong.B: Hiding nutrients would not help plants.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen in a forest if there were no decomposers?
options: Dead leaves would pile up and the soil would lose nutrients
Trees would grow faster than before
It would rain much more often, and rivers would flood the forest
Bread would no longer rise
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead leaves and return nutrients. Without them, dead material would pile up and the soil would get poorer.

wrong.B: With fewer nutrients in the soil, trees would not grow faster.
wrong.C: The article does not connect decomposers to rain.
wrong.D: Yeast makes bread rise. Soil decomposers have nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: As a story told in time order about one scientist
As a list of steps for an experiment
By describing different ways microbes help, one in each paragraph
As a comparison of two kinds of bread
questions.why: After the introduction, each paragraph explains one way microbes help: digestion, bread, yogurt, soil, and medicine.

wrong.A: Two scientists appear, but the article is not one story in time order.
wrong.B: The article does not give steps for an experiment.

questions.stem: What caused the discovery of penicillin?
options: Fleming was baking bread with yeast
Fleming saw that a mold could kill bacteria
Van Leeuwenhoek built a microscope in the 1670s
Farmers found it in the soil
questions.why: The article says Fleming noticed a mold could kill bacteria, and this led to penicillin.

wrong.A: The article does not say Fleming was baking.
wrong.C: Van Leeuwenhoek saw microbes long before penicillin. He did not find it.
wrong.D: The article does not say farmers found penicillin.

questions.stem: Why does the author end by saying microbes are "partners, not enemies"?
options: To show that microbes can think and make plans
To warn readers that microbes are dangerous
To prove that people do not need to wash their hands
To change the idea that all microbes are just bad germs
questions.why: Many people think of microbes only as germs. The article shows how they help, so the ending asks readers to see them differently.

wrong.A: Partners here means helpers. Microbes do not think or plan.
wrong.B: The ending says the opposite: most microbes are not enemies.
wrong.C: The article still tells readers to wash their hands to remove harmful germs.

MID.prompt: Explain how microbes help both people and plants. Use at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I explained how microbes help people.
I explained how microbes help plants.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Microbes, which are so small you need a microscope to see them, help both people and plants in important ways. Most microbes are harmless, and many bacteria that live in your gut help you digest fiber and food your body cannot break down by itself, while also making helpful vitamins. Microbes help plants too, since many microbes in the soil act as a decomposer, breaking down dead leaves and animals and returning important nutrients to the soil so new plants can grow. Because microbes support digestion in people and nutrient cycles for plants, the article calls them valuable partners rather than enemies.

keyWords.definition: a living thing so small it can only be seen with a microscope
keyWords.example: A single drop of seawater can hold thousands of microorganisms.

keyWords.definition: a process in which microbes change sugars into other things, such as gas or acid
keyWords.example: Fermentation gives some foods a sour taste.

keyWords.definition: a living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals into simpler materials
keyWords.example: Without decomposers, fallen branches would stay on the ground for many years.

keyWords.definition: a gas that makes up most of the air; plants need it in a form they can absorb
keyWords.example: Some farmers add nitrogen to their fields to help crops grow.

keyWords.definition: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing
keyWords.example: The doctor said an antibiotic would not help with a cold caused by a virus.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

Although some microbes cause disease, most are harmless and many are essential.

Antibiotics have solved the problem of harmful bacteria forever.

wrong.D: The article warns that bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics.

options: They capture nitrogen from the air and change it into a form plants can use
They keep insects from eating the leaves
They release carbon dioxide that makes the beans swell
They turn the roots into sugar

wrong.B: The article does not mention insects.
wrong.C: Carbon dioxide is described in bread, not in bean roots.
wrong.D: The article does not say bacteria turn roots into sugar.

questions.stem: What did Antonie van Leeuwenhoek contribute, according to the article?
options: He discovered penicillin while working in his laboratory in 1928
He invented the process of fermentation

HIGH.prompt: The article says microbes are "valuable partners rather than enemies." Do you agree? Support your answer with evidence from at least three paragraphs, and explain the article's warning about antibiotics.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the claim.
I used evidence from at least three paragraphs.
I explained why antibiotics should not be overused.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that microbes are valuable partners rather than enemies, because evidence from several paragraphs of the article shows how essential these tiny microorganisms truly are. In the human gut, bacteria digest food we cannot break down ourselves and produce helpful vitamins, while fermentation by yeast and other bacteria gives us risen bread, yogurt, and drinks like laban. In the soil, decomposer microbes break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients such as nitrogen back into the ground so new life can grow, and Alexander Fleming's discovery of a mold that killed bacteria eventually led to penicillin, a medicine that has saved millions of lives. Even so, the article warns that overusing antibiotic medicine can be dangerous, because it can destroy helpful bacteria along with harmful ones and allow stronger germs to survive, which is why people should use antibiotics carefully rather than relying on them too often.
